claims.text: Preferential segregation of Cr and X to the alloy surface governs the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer during exposure above 900 °C.
Surface segregation of Cr and X promotes formation of a dense, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer.
The atomic-size mismatch associated with X modulates diffusion kinetics and oxide-layer stability.
The chemical affinity of X for Cr and oxygen modulates diffusion kinetics and the thermodynamic stability of the oxide layer.
Atomic-size mismatch and chemical affinity enhance selective oxidation of Cr and X.
Selective oxidation of Cr and X leads to a dense, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer.
The dense, adherent oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier that limits further oxidation.
The dense, adherent oxide layer prevents oxide spallation.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiAl will form more stable and coherent protective oxide layers than CrFeCoNiMn.
The predicted advantage of Si and Al over Mn arises from their stronger affinity for oxygen.
Si and Al can form more thermodynamically stable oxides than Mn in the proposed alloy and exposure context.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiAl will show less oxide cracking or spallation than CrFeCoNiMn.
CrFeCoNi without X is expected to form a less stable and less adherent oxide layer than the Si- or Al-containing alloys under the same conditions.
The proposed hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
The proposed hypothesis is bounded to oxidative or corrosive exposure above 900 °C.
A comparison at 1000 °C for 100 hours can test the predicted oxide composition, morphology, and adherence differences.
